# The Department of Almost

The Department of Almost occupied the fourth floor of a building that had never received its final coat of paint. From the street, it looked less like a government office than a thought someone had been interrupted while having.

Mara found it on a Thursday, after the rain had stopped but before the city had decided whether to dry.

She had been carrying the letter for eleven years.

It was not a remarkable letter. Three pages, blue ink, an envelope softened at the corners. She had written it to her brother during the last winter of their mother’s life, and she had never sent it. Then her brother had moved, and then she had moved, and then not sending it had become a kind of arrangement.

The department’s address appeared on the back of a receipt from a bakery she did not remember entering.

**For matters nearly settled**, it said.

Inside the building, the lift offered buttons for floors one, two, three, and eventually.

Mara took the stairs.

On the fourth-floor landing stood a rubber plant, a clock without a minute hand, and a receptionist eating an orange with great concentration.

“I’m not sure I belong here,” Mara said.

The receptionist placed a strip of peel on a napkin.

“That’s our most common opening statement.”

“I have a letter.”

“Sent or unsent?”

“Unsent.”

“Good. Sent letters are downstairs, in Consequences.”

She slid a form across the desk.

At the top, in neat black type, it read:

**WHAT WERE YOU ABOUT TO DO?**

---

The waiting room contained six people and an aquarium full of water.

No fish. Just water, circulating faithfully through a little stone castle.

A young man in a wedding suit held a single running shoe. An elderly woman had brought a cake under a glass dome. Beside the window, a boy was trying to remember a tune, producing the same five notes over and over.

Mara sat near a man whose briefcase was leaking sand.

“First visit?” he asked.

She nodded.

“Don’t agree to a permanent solution straight away.”

“What kind of solution?”

He tilted the briefcase upright.

“I nearly became a geologist.”

Before she could ask what that meant, a door opened and a clerk called her name.

The clerk was tall and narrow, with sleeves rolled to precisely equal heights. His identification badge read **ELIAS, PROVISIONAL**.

His office contained two chairs, a desk, and shelves of objects that seemed unconnected: a chipped mug, a ballet slipper, a tiny brass cannon, a jar of dark water.

“Please,” he said, indicating the chair without a stack of newspapers on it.

Mara placed the letter on his desk.

Elias did not touch it.

“What outcome are you seeking?”

“I thought you might tell me.”

“That’s possible, but expensive.”

“How expensive?”

“Usually several years.”

Mara almost smiled.

“I’d like to stop carrying this around.”

“In your bag?”

“In general.”

He nodded, as if the distinction mattered.

“Before we proceed,” he said, “I should explain that we do not remove the past. We have tried. It affects the plumbing.”

---

Elias opened a drawer and took out a small wooden tray.

“Set it here.”

Mara laid the letter in the tray. The envelope shifted slightly, like something settling into sleep.

“How does the department work?” she asked.

“Unfinished actions accumulate. Most disperse naturally. You consider buying pears, buy apples instead, and the pear intention evaporates by supper. But certain things persist.”

“Because they matter?”

“Sometimes because they matter. Sometimes because they were interrupted at an unfortunate angle.”

He gestured toward the shelves.

“That mug belongs to a woman who was about to ask her husband whether he was happy.”

“What happened?”

“The kettle boiled.”

“And then?”

“Thirty-seven years.”

Mara looked at the mug.

It was ordinary white ceramic, with a faded picture of a duck.

“Did she ever ask?”

“She came here last month.”

“What did you do?”

“Helped her decide whether she still wanted the answer.”

From somewhere beyond the wall came the sound of applause, abruptly cut off.

“Unmade speeches,” Elias explained.

“Do you keep everything here?”

“Certainly not. We’d need a much larger building. We maintain representative objects. The rest is stored in the city.”

“Where?”

“Wherever there’s room. The pause before a traffic light changes. The space under an unused chair. The last second of a song after someone turns off the radio.”

Mara glanced at the letter.

“So this has been taking up space?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

Elias put on his glasses.

“That’s what we’re about to find out.”

---

He unfolded the pages carefully.

Mara watched his eyes move.

She remembered writing the letter at her kitchen table, beside a bowl of oranges going soft. She remembered the thrill of arranging her anger so that it looked like evidence. Every paragraph had seemed reasonable. Every reasonable paragraph had contained a concealed knife.

Her brother, Daniel, had not visited enough.

He had not called enough.

He had said their mother sounded better on the telephone because he could not hear what it cost her to sound that way.

All this was true.

There were other true things she had left out.

Elias finished reading.

“Well?” Mara said.

“It’s a very efficient letter.”

“That sounds bad.”

“It accomplishes several things at once. It accuses him, defends you, remembers your mother, and requests an apology without admitting that an apology is what you want.”

Mara folded her arms.

“You said you weren’t going to tell me what outcome I wanted.”

“I said it was expensive.”

He turned the last page toward her.

At the bottom, beneath her signature, was a sentence she did not remember writing.

**You were supposed to know I needed you.**

The ink looked fresh.

“That wasn’t there.”

“No,” Elias said.

“Did you write it?”

“No.”

She touched the words. They did not smear.

For eleven years she had remembered the letter as a record of Daniel’s failures. The new sentence made her want to take it back from Elias.

Outside, a bus hissed at the curb.

---

“There are three standard options,” Elias said.

He took out a brochure so old that the woman pictured on its cover was holding a telephone attached to a wall.

“Completion, release, or conversion.”

“What’s conversion?”

“We turn the unfinished matter into something else.”

“Such as?”

“A garden. An unreasonable dislike of a particular song. Expertise in restoring antique clocks. It depends on the material.”

“And release?”

“You accept that it will remain unfinished.”

“That sounds like doing nothing.”

“It can look similar from a distance.”

Mara stood and went to the window.

Below, a cyclist waited at a red light despite there being no cars. A delivery driver rearranged parcels in a van.

“I can’t send that letter,” she said.

“You can.”

“It would be cruel.”

“Possibly.”

“And it’s too late.”

“For that version of the conversation, certainly.”

She turned.

“What does that mean?”

Elias considered her.

“Would you like to see storage?”

“Will it help?”

“I don’t know. But most people find the brochure disappointing.”

He lifted the wooden tray. The letter had become heavier; Mara could tell by the adjustment of his wrists.

They went through a door behind his desk into a narrow passage lined with coat hooks.

Each hook held a different shadow.

“Unaccepted invitations,” Elias said.

One shadow raised a hand as they passed.

Mara nearly raised hers back.

At the end of the passage, Elias unlocked a green door with a key that looked freshly cut.

Beyond it was an enormous railway station.

---

The station roof vanished into a bright, overcast distance.

Platforms extended in every direction. Some held trains. Others held houses, dinner tables, hospital beds, or stretches of empty road.

There were announcements, but Mara could understand only fragments.

“Passengers intending to explain themselves—”

“Due to an unexpected act of kindness—”

“The service originally scheduled for last November—”

On the nearest platform, a man repeatedly approached a woman sitting on a bench. Each time he came within a few steps, the scene reset. He was back beside a vending machine, adjusting his coat.

“Is he trapped?”

“No. He’s at home watching television. This is the approach he never made.”

“Who is she?”

“Someone he thought he recognized.”

“Did he?”

“We don’t collect outcomes that never happened.”

They walked past a field where a house had been marked out with stakes and string. Past a classroom full of raised hands. Past a restaurant in which a waiter held a bottle above two empty glasses.

Then Mara saw a kitchen.

Her mother’s kitchen.

The yellow curtains were there, and the calendar from the insurance company, and the burn mark on the counter shaped vaguely like a country.

Daniel stood beside the sink.

He was younger than she remembered him being, which unsettled her.

“What is this?”

Elias looked at the tray.

“An associated matter.”

In the kitchen, Daniel took a telephone from his pocket.

He looked at its screen.

He put it away.

Then he took it out again.

---

“That doesn’t prove anything,” Mara said.

“No.”

“He could have been calling anyone.”

“Yes.”

Daniel leaned against the sink. Through the kitchen doorway, Mara could see the narrow bed they had brought downstairs for their mother.

She remembered that afternoon.

She had gone to the pharmacy, then driven past the house and parked beside the river. She had sat there for forty minutes with the medicine on the passenger seat.

When she returned, Daniel said he had to leave.

She had hated him for having somewhere to go.

In the station kitchen, he pressed something on the telephone and lifted it to his ear.

The scene stopped.

“Can you make it continue?” Mara asked.

“This is where the unfinished part ends.”

“But what was he going to say?”

“We don’t know.”

“Surely someone knows.”

“Perhaps your brother.”

She watched his still face. He looked exhausted. She had forgotten that, or had never noticed.

It did not cancel anything. He had left. She had stayed. Their mother had needed things in the night, and Mara had been the person who heard.

She waited for the scene to provide more: a message on the screen, a word from him, something she could use.

Nothing moved.

“People sometimes stay here for hours,” Elias said.

“Does it change?”

“No.”

Mara glanced at him, annoyed by how gently he had answered.

“I’d like to go back.”

He turned toward the green door, carrying the tray between them, and she followed without looking into any of the other platforms.

---

Back in the office, Elias put the letter on the desk.

Mara sat with her coat still on.

“Does your family know what you do?” she asked.

“My daughter thinks I work in permits.”

“Do you have unfinished things?”

“Of course.”

“Can’t you fix them?”

“Being employed here is not the same as being good at it.”

He straightened the brochure.

“I have been meaning to apologize to a friend for nine years.”

“What happened?”

“I was funny at his expense in a room where he needed me to be kind.”

“Why haven’t you?”

“For a while I thought explaining my intentions would help. Then I realized I was waiting until I could apologize without feeling ashamed.”

He put the brochure back in the drawer.

Mara took her telephone from her bag.

Daniel’s number was still there.

They exchanged birthday messages. At Christmas, photographs. He had a dog she had never met and a wife she liked but did not know well enough to telephone independently.

Once, two years earlier, he had sent a picture of a badly assembled bookshelf.

**Mum would have called this modern**, he wrote.

Mara had replied with a laughing face.

She remembered almost adding something else.

Now she opened their messages.

The blank field looked very small.

“What should I say?”

Elias shook his head.

“That part isn’t a service we provide.”

She typed, deleted, and typed again.

**I found an old letter I wrote to you. I don’t think I should send it. But could we talk about that winter sometime?**

She read it twice.

Then she pressed send.

---

Nothing happened.

The shelves did not tremble. The jar of dark water remained dark. Somewhere outside the office, a printer jammed.

Mara looked at the screen.

“I thought—”

“Yes,” Elias said. “People often do.”

“Was that completion?”

“That was a message.”

She laughed, unexpectedly, and had to wipe her eyes.

He passed her a box of tissues without commenting.

After a while she asked what would happen if Daniel did not answer.

“You’ll decide what to do then.”

“And if he answers badly?”

“The same.”

The letter lay between them.

She had imagined, without admitting it, that relinquishing it would make the eleven years available again. There would be some relief large enough to account for the time.

Instead, she was tired. She needed lunch. She had sent her brother a message she could no longer edit.

She folded the pages and returned them to the envelope.

“I think I’ll keep it for now.”

“All right.”

“Is that allowed?”

“It belongs to you.”

When Elias handed it over, it felt like three sheets of paper.

At reception, the woman was clearing away her orange peel.

“Settled?” she asked.

“Not yet.”

The receptionist nodded and reached for the next form.

Mara went down the stairs. On the second-floor landing, she stopped to check her telephone. There was no reply.

She put it in her bag rather than carrying it in her hand.

Outside, water was still dripping from the scaffolding. She stepped around a puddle and went looking for somewhere to eat.

---

Daniel called that evening while Mara was washing a pan.

She let it ring twice, dried her hands, and answered.

“Hello.”

“Hello,” he said.

For a moment, both listened.

Then Daniel said, “Is this a bad time?”

“No.”

“You’re sure?”

“The pan can wait.”

He laughed. It was the same laugh, older.

They did not settle everything. Daniel remembered some things differently. He said something defensive, and Mara answered sharply. There was a silence during which she considered ending the call.

Then he asked, “What was in the letter?”

She sat down.

“Some things I still mean,” she said. “Some things I wouldn’t say now.”

“Will you tell me?”

So she began.

Later, she would remember the conversation imperfectly. She would remember the refrigerator switching on. A car door outside. Daniel telling her that on the afternoon she went to the pharmacy, he had nearly called to ask her to come home.

“Why didn’t you?”

“I thought you needed a break.”

“I did.”

“I know.”

“No,” she said, then stopped. “I don’t think you did.”

This time, he let her explain.

They spoke until the kitchen window reflected only the room.

The following week, Mara passed the unfinished building. A dentist occupied the fourth floor. On the landing below, someone had left a rubber plant with a note asking whoever took it to give it plenty of light.

She carried it home on the bus.

It fitted beside her kitchen window.

She watered it, then moved the letter to a drawer.
